You're not out of ideas — you've just been working inside a fairly narrow band lately (abstract bold-color geometry, Monet-style watercolor, and the palette-knife texture stuff). The quickest way out is to borrow from a different part of your own life, not to paint more of the same. A few directions that fit what you're already drawn to:

**Paint the Frida Kahlo & Diego Rivera show before you've even seen it.** You're already planning to go to that Mexican Modernism exhibit at the City Art Museum, and you've got a real interest in women artists and Kahlo specifically. Kahlo's work is the opposite of your current abstract/geometric stuff — dense symbolism, saturated color, flat decorative pattern, and self-portraiture. Even just studying a few pieces and copying one small detail (a hand, a motif, a color pairing) would pull you out of your usual mode.

**Try nocturnes.** You're into night photography — star trails, city lights, the Mission District with street art in the foreground. Painting light at night is a fresh subject for you, and it lets you use the long-exposure "how light behaves" eye you've been building in photography. A single street scene at night, or a star-trail sky over a cityscape, would be genuinely new territory.

**Use your own photos as reference.** Your photography project is all about mixing urban and natural elements, textures, and architecture. You already have a personal library of interesting backdrops — that's a ready-made inspiration source you're not using for the paintings. Pick a photo you loved and paint from it.

**Commit one painting to a specific place you're about to go.** Red Rock Canyon in June is close and has a dramatically different palette (rust, ochre, hard shadow) from anything you've painted. Or the North Cascades, or even the saturated color and pattern of Punjab folk dance from your India trip. Giving yourself "this one is about X place" is a constraint that breaks the stuck feeling.

One more thing worth naming: part of the "stuck" may be the texture. You've said the impasto/drybrushing still isn't clicking, and that friction can make everything feel flat. A change of subject (like the night scene or a Kahlo study) often unblocks the technique more than grinding on the same one does — you stop fighting the medium and start following the image.
